lessons.title: Five vowels inside consonant–vowel patterns
lessons.objective: Change Spanish vowel shape inside ma mi mu me mo, then transfer the same movements into other consonant rows and real words.
lessons.explanation:
Keep each vowel clear inside ma mi mu me mo. Notice the tongue moving forward for mi and back with rounded lips for mu.
The m row
ma · me · mi · mo · mu
Close both lips for m, then open into the vowel. These are practice syllables, not five vocabulary words.
lips
Both lips meet
The tongue prepares for the next vowel; the lips make the closure.
Air passes through the nose during m.
Voice on
Say mmm → ma, then me, mi, mo, mu. Open from the same light lip closure each time.
Keep the nasal m audible before the vowel.

lessons.title: The p row
lessons.objective: Practise a brief p release with less aspiration than a stressed English p.
lessons.explanation:
Make a small lip closure and release into pa pi pu pe po. Keep the vowels distinct without a strong English-style puff.
The p row
pa · pe · pi · po · pu
Close both lips, release, then say the vowel. Avoid a strong English-style puff of air.
lips
Both lips meet, then release
The tongue prepares for the vowel. Keep the lip closure brief.
Briefly stop oral airflow, then release.
Voice off for the consonant

lessons.title: The t row
lessons.objective: Find Spanish dental t placement.
lessons.explanation:

ta · te · ti · to · tu

teeth

Use a light contact near the back of the upper teeth; release into the vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ta → ti → tu slowly. Notice the dental contact rather than an English-style ridge contact.
Avoid a strong puff or an extra vowel after t.

lessons.title: The n and l rows
lessons.objective: Keep the consonant distinct while changing vowels.
lessons.explanation:
Alternate na ni nu ne no and la li lu le lo. Keep nasal airflow for n and side airflow for l while the vowel changes.
The n row
na · ne · ni · no · nu
Let air pass through the nose for n, then move into the vowel.
ridge
Tongue tip at the ridge behind the upper front teeth
Make a light closure; prepare the next vowel without pressing hard.
Air passes through the nose during n.
Voice on
Say nnn → na, then na → ni → nu. Release the tongue into each vowel.
Connected speech can move the contact place; that comes in the Core lessons.
The l row
la · le · li · lo · lu
Touch the ridge behind the upper teeth with the tongue tip; let air pass around the sides.
ridge
Tongue tip near the ridge; sides leave space for airflow
Keep a light central tongue contact while air escapes at the sides.
Oral airflow around the sides of the tongue.
Voice on
Say la → li → lu, then lado → lima → luna. Notice the vowel change without losing the l.
Do not add an extra vowel before the l.

lessons.title: The s and f rows
lessons.objective: Carry a continuous consonant into a steady vowel.
lessons.explanation:
Keep continuous airflow through sa si su se so and fa fi fu fe fo. Use the tongue groove for s and light lip-to-teeth narrowing for f.
The s row
sa · se · si · so · su
Make a continuous s, then move into the vowel. Later lessons introduce regional variation in syllable-final s.
ridge
Tongue approaches the ridge; a narrow channel remains
Do not seal the mouth; form a groove and leave space for airflow.
Continuous oral airflow.
Voice off
Say sss → sa, then sa → si → su. Keep the beginning continuous.
This is a narrowing target, not a complete contact. Syllable-final s varies regionally.
The f row
fa · fe · fi · fo · fu
Rest the lower lip lightly at the upper front teeth and let air flow through the narrow gap.
lip-teeth
Upper front teeth near the lower lip
Leave a small opening instead of biting the lip.
Continuous oral airflow through the gap.
Voice off
Say fff → fa, then fa → fi → fu with a gentle, continuous beginning.
Keep the lip contact light and the airflow steady.

lessons.objective: Coordinate the back-of-tongue closure and vowel transition in /k/ patterns, then transfer into clear words and phrases.

Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ka → ki → ku → ke → ko slowly. Start each vowel with a small tongue-back closure and release; avoid a large English-style puff.
Do not use the tongue tip for k. The closure location adjusts naturally with the vowel.

lessons.title: Ch, ñ, and vowel review
lessons.objective: Build ch and ñ from a model without turning them into letter names.
lessons.explanation:
Coordinate the brief closure and friction in ch, then the palatal nasal in ñ. Use cha chi chu che cho and ña ñi ñu ñe ño before real words.
The ch row
cha · che · chi · cho · chu
Begin with a brief closure and release into a ch sound. Practise the syllables, then use meaningful words.
postalveolar
Tongue blade just behind the ridge
Begin with a brief closure, then release into a narrow passage.
Brief blockage followed by friction.
Voice off
Say cha once, then cha → chi → chu. Keep closure and friction as one coordinated sound.
Do not separate it into two spoken syllables.
The ñ row
ña · ñe · ñi · ño · ñu
Raise the tongue body toward the hard palate and let air flow through the nose; then release into the vowel.
palate
Tongue body toward the hard palate
Use a palatal nasal gesture rather than a separate n plus an added syllable.
Air passes through the nose.
Voice on
Say ña slowly, then ña → ñi → ñu; move into mañana and niño with a model.
The tongue-body target matters more than an English spelling approximation.

ba · be · bi · bo · bu

lips

Voice on

The letters b and v normally belong to the same sound family; contextual variants need their own examples.

lessons.title: Dental t and d
lessons.objective: Place both sounds near the upper teeth and compare voicing.
lessons.explanation:
Compare ta ti tu te to with da di du de do. Keep a light dental contact and notice the voicing difference instead of pressing harder.
The t row
ta · te · ti · to · tu
Place the tongue tip against the back of the upper front teeth. Release into the vowel without a strong puff of air.
teeth
Tongue tip/blade at the upper front teeth
Use a light contact near the back of the upper teeth; release into the vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ta → ti → tu slowly. Notice the dental contact rather than an English-style ridge contact.
Avoid a strong puff or an extra vowel after t.
The /d/ family
da · de · di · do · du
Begin after a pause with the tongue near the back of the upper teeth. Between vowels the closure often becomes a light narrowing.
teeth
Tongue tip/blade near the upper front teeth
After a pause use a light closure. Between vowels, compare a more open gesture in a model phrase.
Closure or narrow oral passage, depending on context.
Voice on
Say da after a pause, then cada día. Notice that the contact may be lighter within the phrase.
The sound can change with context without changing its written letter.

lessons.objective: Match rhythm and intonation to a courteous request.

The p row
pa · pe · pi · po · pu

lessons.title: Repair and clarification
lessons.objective: Clarify a message naturally when misunderstood.
lessons.explanation:
Warm up with da di du de do. Repair only the part that caused difficulty, changing pace or wording while preserving the intended meaning.
The /d/ family
da · de · di · do · du
Begin after a pause with the tongue near the back of the upper teeth. Between vowels the closure often becomes a light narrowing.
teeth
Tongue tip/blade near the upper front teeth
After a pause use a light closure. Between vowels, compare a more open gesture in a model phrase.
Closure or narrow oral passage, depending on context.
Voice on
Say da after a pause, then cada día. Notice that the contact may be lighter within the phrase.
The sound can change with context without changing its written letter.

lessons.title: Regional y/ll listening
lessons.objective: Recognize examples from named regions without mixing every feature.
lessons.explanation:
Keep a consistent production model for y/ll and compare named regional examples only when real reviewed audio is available. Without those clips, use this as a transcript and discussion task, not a listening test.
Y and ll in a yeísta model
ya · ye · yi · yo · yu
Raise the front/body of the tongue toward the hard palate. The precise realization depends on context and region; yi uses an uncommon anchor word.
palate
Tongue body approaches the hard palate
Follow the chosen regional model: constriction and friction vary.
Oral airflow with a region/context-specific constriction.
Usually voiced in the reference family; regional models differ
Say ya → yo → yu with one named speaker model, then yate → yo → yuca.
Do not mark valid Río de la Plata realizations or ll-preserving varieties as inherently wrong.

lessons.title: Regional s and j listening
lessons.objective: Recognize selected variations in real, reviewed recordings.
lessons.explanation:
Compare regional s and j only with identified speaker examples. Keep the consonant-linked production pattern; do not teach dropping consonants as a universal shortcut to sounding natural.
J and g before e/i
ja · je · ji · jo · ju
Use a back-of-mouth narrowing with airflow. The degree and location of friction vary by region; some models use a lighter h-like sound.
velar
Back-of-mouth narrowing; region-dependent
For a velar model, raise the tongue back toward the soft palate without a complete seal.
Continuous airflow; friction can be stronger or lighter by region.
Voice off
Say ja → ji → ju gently using the chosen model, then jamón → jirafa → jugo.
Do not force harsh throat friction; a lighter realization can be regional rather than an error.

lessons.title: Personal sound priorities
lessons.objective: Choose two recurring pronunciation habits from real evidence.
lessons.explanation:
Select two priorities from real self-listening or instructor observations. Use the relevant consonant-linked row, then test the movement in a new phrase instead of drilling everything faster.
The m row
ma · me · mi · mo · mu
Close both lips for m, then open into the vowel. These are practice syllables, not five vocabulary words.
lips
Both lips meet
The tongue prepares for the next vowel; the lips make the closure.
Air passes through the nose during m.
Voice on
Say mmm → ma, then me, mi, mo, mu. Open from the same light lip closure each time.
Keep the nasal m audible before the vowel.

lessons.title: Conversation under a complication
lessons.objective: Maintain clear speech when a scene changes unexpectedly.
lessons.explanation:
Warm up with ka ki ku ke ko, then handle a complication without a script. Preserve the important consonants, numbers, and phrase boundaries while deciding what to do.
The /k/ sound row
ca · que · qui · co · cu
One sound, different spellings: c before a/o/u; qu before e/i. The u in que and qui is silent.
velar
Back of tongue meets the soft palate, then releases
Keep the tongue tip relaxed while the tongue back closes and releases into the next vowel.
Brief oral blockage, then release.
Voice off for the consonant
Say ka → ki → ku → ke → ko slowly. Start each vowel with a small tongue-back closure and release; avoid a large English-style puff.
Do not use the tongue tip for k. The closure location adjusts naturally with the vowel.

lessons.title: Final transfer portfolio
lessons.objective: Compare baseline and final speech using a clear review rubric.
lessons.explanation:
Choose your own consonant-linked warm-up, then compare baseline and final speech with specific observations. Use a new reading and an unexpected question; completion alone is not an assessed native accent.
Initial r and rr
ra · re · ri · ro · ru
Let a relaxed tongue tip respond to airflow near the ridge. Build toward the trill gradually; pressing harder is not the goal.
ridge
Tongue tip near the ridge, with repeated vibration
Keep the tip relaxed and allow airflow to drive the vibration.
Oral airflow supports repeated brief tongue contacts.
Voice on
Alternate a relaxed ra attempt with the word rama; pause between attempts. Use the model before adding speed.
A trill is not a tightly held tongue press. Mark it as developing if a clear trill is not yet available.
